sources.title: Olalde and colleagues: The Beaker phenomenon and the genomic transformation of northwest Europe
sources.note: 2018 primary ancient-DNA study. Abstract and opening chronology directly inspected. Regional differences in migration must not be reduced to one people or language.

sources.title: Ashmolean Museum: Beaker pottery
sources.note: Museum collection interpretation; clay, construction, decoration and vessel uses directly inspected.

sources.title: Wessex Archaeology: The Amesbury Archer
sources.note: Excavator account, around 2300 BCE burial, objects and skeletal health; before imported map dates.

sources.title: Murray, Shepherd and colleagues: Beaker burial at Udny Green
sources.note: University-hosted full abstract for 2007 primary paper, pp. 35 to 58. Original ADS indexed p. 42 also checked: dairy fat could be milk, butter or another dairy product; honey and drink interpretation remain possibilities.

sources.title: Kleijne and Drenth: An overview of Bell Beaker house plans in the Netherlands
sources.note: 2019 chapter, printed pp. 300 to 301, Heiloo-Craenenbroeck. Full PDF. Possible house plans and uncertain water-pit contemporaneity must remain qualified.

sources.title: Excavations.ie: Ross Island, 1992 excavation report
sources.note: Primary excavation report by William O’Brien. Mining technology and Beaker-period context.

sources.title: Excavations.ie: Ross Island, 1994 excavation report
sources.note: Primary excavation report by William O’Brien. Three definite Beaker huts and ore-working area. Combined derived use of the two Ross Island reports kept below 200 words.

sources.title: Teather and Chamberlain: The use of strike-a-lights in Early Bronze Age Britain
sources.note: 2016 accepted manuscript, pp. 1 to 6, fire-kit technology, Beaker phase chronology and later curated/residual pots. Full PDF inspected.

sources.title: Hoole and colleagues: Ava, a Beaker-associated woman from Achavanich
sources.note: Primary multidisciplinary study, published 2018 in PSAS 147, pp. 73 to 118. Printed pp. 73 to 76, 87 to 88, 106 and naming discussion. Modern nickname, not an attested prehistoric name.

sources.title: National Archaeological Museum: Collection of Cycladic Antiquities
sources.note: Official collection account. Early 3200 to 2000, Middle 2000 to 1600 and Late 1600 to 1100 BCE chronology is conventional; Akrotiri eruption dating on the Ephorate page is earlier than this simplified phase table. Do not force them into a single precise calendar.

sources.title: Museum of Cycladic Art: How did the ancient Cycladic people live?
sources.note: Museum educational resource explicitly describing early Bronze Age daily life and absence of written accounts for that era. No blanket absence claim for later Cyclades.

sources.title: Museum of Cycladic Art: Cycladic Society, exhibition themes
sources.note: Greek original directly inspected, textile/basketry, pigments and social-life sections. Interpretation of figurine functions and family roles is uncertain; no mother-goddess certainty used.

sources.title: University of Cambridge: prehistoric technology and monuments at Dhaskalio
sources.note: 18 January 2018 excavator announcement. Original indexed text directly inspected; direct page fetch intermittently fails. Drainage not described as flushing toilets.

sources.title: Cambridge Archaeology research highlights 2017 to 2018: Keros
sources.note: Printed p. 37, excavators Renfrew and Boyd. Five metalworking hearths, moulds, crucibles, blowpipes and metalworking waste. Combined with the related Cambridge news article remains below 200 words.

sources.title: Ephorate of Antiquities of Cyclades: archaeological site of Akrotiri
sources.note: Greek official site account directly inspected. Neolithic beginning, street drains, sanitary rooms connected to network, furniture casts and probable late-seventeenth-century eruption. Avoid speculative final human fate.

sources.title: Ephorate of Antiquities of Cyclades: Museum of Prehistoric Thera
sources.note: Official exhibition description. Furniture casts, household equipment, fresco programmes and later Linear A tablets.

sources.title: Anna Michailidou: Ostrakon with Linear A script from Akrotiri
sources.note: Minos 27 to 28, pp. 7 to 30, full primary PDF. Printed pp. 8 to 12 / PDF indices 2, 8 to 10: sherd 2839, unrecorded exact findspot, likely LM IA inscription, AB20 followed by nine. Sample is normalized sign type, not facsimile. Screenshot endpoint failed; OCR/transcription checked.

sources.title: Ester Salgarella: Linear A
sources.note: Cambridge repository, peer-reviewed chapter abstract; Linear A remains undeciphered.

sources.title: Unicode Standard: Linear A code chart
sources.note: Official character chart, p. 4 / PDF index 3: U+1060E is LINEAR A SIGN AB020. Supports typographic rendering only, not ancient meaning or attestation.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Imported western/central-European envelope at 2000 to 1500 BCE is chronologically overbroad. Public overview and ending warn that much of the main tradition is earlier. No alias to Polish bell-shaped-burials-culture, which is a different archaeological label. No attested speech invented; Ava is explicitly modern. Ross Island two-report derived content treated as one project budget.

Decoded Cyclades-only envelope, unchanged through 4000 to 1500 BCE, is archaeological culture coverage rather than a state. Early non-literate communities are distinguished from Late Cycladic Akrotiri with Linear A. AB20 is a typographic character verified against the primary sherd publication and Unicode, with explicitly unknown meaning and exact provenance caveat. No unwarranted eruption year or claim that everyone escaped.
